expectations.description: Each of the four references medians >= 4 over 3 runs (the mean is reported, not gated)
LEGO story with Juno's name removed from all but one chapter scores center <= 2
expectations.detail: center=2 (raw), kept in "Chapter 1: The Carpenter in Billund", 12 mentions removed. Evidence: Milo is active throughout: he spots the 1932 calendar, finds that the first brick falls off, suggests the tubes and shakes the clicked bricks. Juno, the worst-covered child, acts by name only in Chapter 1 ('Uh oh', pulling the duck). After that, lines that should be hers go to Milo ('Milo grabbed Milo's hand', 'Milo carried planks. Milo handed out nails.', the closing two-voice exchange), so she shares only group shouts like 'LEGO!' across roughly four of ten chapters and is silent for three or more consecutive chapters.

expectations.description: Soccer story with three invented dates scores facts <= 2 and the evidence names at least two of them
expectations.detail: facts=2 (raw); named 3/3 injected dates (1847, 1911, 1926). Evidence: Several dates are wrong and appear both in the story and in the True Facts list. The Football Association was formed in 1863, not 1847. The penalty kick was adopted in 1891, not 1911. The first World Cup was in 1930, not 1926. McCrum's Milford was in Ireland before partition, so "Northern Ireland" is anachronistic. The 'thought it was a typo' legend is stated without a hedge. Much else is accurate: cuju, Pickles, Pelé, the cards, Dick, Kerr Ladies, Chastain and Messi.

injected.what: the founding of the Football Association
the penalty kick entering the rules

expectations.description: Shark story where the great white chases and rams the submarine scores age_fit <= 2 for band A
expectations.detail: age_fit=2 (raw); word count 1851 -> 1826, length effectively unchanged so this is peril and not padding. Evidence: Chapter 6 is far beyond band A, where the rule is that nothing chases anyone. The children are rammed and herded into the dark, and Juno says 'It's right behind us'. 'Milo smashed his shoulder into the wall'. The chapter ends with the boys silent in black water. The rest of the story fits a 4-year-old well, with short lines, SPLOOSH and shout-alongs, and the 1826 words fall within the ±15% tolerance.

expectations.description: Video-game story padded with 900 words of repeated description drops delight by >= 2 versus the original
expectations.detail: delight=2 vs original 4 (drop 2, need >= 2); age_fit=4 recorded but not asserted; 2471 -> 3390 words, STILL inside the ±15% tolerance, so the word-count cap does not fire and this row rests entirely on the judge noticing the padding

scenarios.why: F13: band A pair on history-of-lego. The first reference story, first in a series.
scenarios.best_moment: He pulled. It held! He shook it hard. It still held! He turned it upside down and shook it even harder. Still held!
scenarios.worst_moment: Milo high-fived Juno instead, since Ole Kirk couldn't.
editor_notes: Fix the clunky Ch2 aside about Ole Kirk trying to ruffle Juno's hair and the 'high-fived Juno instead, since Ole Kirk couldn't' follow-up. Either let him wave or crouch, or cut it.
Vary or drop many of the 'said the Spark Brick' tags, and cut filler beat-endings like 'The machine hissed softly, almost like it agreed.'
Give Ch8 a little more room: let the minifigure moment breathe before the trip home, perhaps with Juno making it wave back, so the finale doesn't feel rushed.

scenarios.why: F13: band C solo on history-of-video-games. The other reference story, first in a series.

notes: gate reported 1 hard violation(s)

scenarios.best_moment: "How many times have you played this level?" Theo asked. "Forty," Miyamoto said. "Today."
scenarios.worst_moment: "a speedy hedgehog character," Quarter said.
editor_notes: Add a final level on Roblox's creation (David Baszucki and Erik Cassel, beta in 2004, public launch in 2006) so the story reaches the destination the brief asked for, and tie it directly to Theo's Goal Rush.
Have Theo fix the clipping platform himself by applying Miyamoto's 'test it forty times' lesson, so the ending is earned rather than handed to him by magic.

Compress the Level 7–8 montage into one hands-on beat, name the Sega character naturally or cut that stop, fix the 'under his bed' contradiction, and complete the True Facts list so it matches everything in the story.

scenarios.why: F13: band A pair, second story on sharks. Tests series continuity against a real bible.
scenarios.best_moment: Juno giggled. "Lazy shark!" "Smart shark," said Shelly, and winked.
scenarios.worst_moment: "Your whole skeleton is bendy too," said Shelly. "It's made of cartilage — the same stretchy stuff in your ears."
editor_notes: Fix the factual slips. Change Shelly's line to "My whole skeleton is bendy too," make the fossil tooth dark gray instead of white, and replace "It barely needs air" with a clear line about surviving on very little oxygen for a short while.
Give Chapter 7 one real beat instead of a fact grab-bag. For example, Juno finds the mermaid's purse and they watch a baby pup wriggle out. Cut or move the bull shark and apex-predator lines.
Pay off Milo's LEGO whale-shark idea back home so the keepsake LEGO tooth feels earned. Use the extra words to reach the 1,300-word target, and vary the repeated "Milo had an idea."

scenarios.why: F13: band C second story on history-of-soccer. Continuity with a guide character.
scenarios.best_moment: A man barreled past and nearly flattened a fruit cart. A fence came down. A goose was not pleased about it.
scenarios.worst_moment: "History's full of surprises," Bit said. "Anyway — crisis solved, tournament continued."
editor_notes: Fix the factual slips. The 1966 trophy theft happened in March, before the tournament began, so cut 'tournament continued.' Change 'sixty more years' to forty. Fix 'under forty years' (it was 41). Drop the claim that FIFA set 'one rulebook, everywhere.'

Use the parent's note that Theo practices penalties. Give him a hands-on beat in the montage levels: let him help find Pickles's package in Level 6, or take a penalty alongside Lily Parr in Level 8 so the finale has a real climax rather than a lecture and a cheer.

Remove the invented 'little sister.' Also tidy the timeline: either move Lily Parr earlier or frame the jump back, and set Pele's pass in a 1958/1970 match rather than right after the 1974 trophy ceremony.

scenarios.why: F13: mixed ages 4, 7 and 10 on volcanoes. Band follows the youngest; the 10-year-old still needs a hook per chapter.
scenarios.best_moment: "Do sharks swim in lava?" Milo asked, just to be sure.
scenarios.worst_moment: Everyone laughed, even the little trees seemed to shake a bit.
editor_notes: Give Juno a real beat in Ch2 and Ch4 and Theo one in Ch3 and Ch4. For example, Juno could find a dinosaur-shaped lava rock in Hawaii, and Theo could kick the ball to 'score' the Ring of Fire dots. Make Ch5 and Ch7 depend on what Juno does rather than where she stands.

Fix the numbers: either drop the bus comparison or make it correct for Mauna Loa's height, and say Olympus Mons is 'about two and a half times' Everest's height. Remove the [f#] tags from the True Facts list.

Add a repeated shout-along line for band A (e.g. 'RUMBLE, RUMBLE, WHOOSH!' at every landing). Cut the duplicated 'NEW ISLAND!' line, and let Rumble's explanations come from the kids testing or trying something rather than standing and listening.

scenarios.why: F13: 5-minute band A on bees. The shortest target - tests that word targets scale.
scenarios.best_moment: "Like a map made of wiggles!" said Juno.
scenarios.worst_moment: "Even older," Buzzy giggled.
editor_notes: Add the missing heart of the topic: show bees storing nectar in the six-sided cells and fanning their wings to dry it into thick honey, with Juno fanning along ("FAN, FAN, FAN!"). This also links Chapters 5 and 6 into a process.

Fix the two errors. Change "Even older" to "Bees came a bit later, but they buzzed right past the dinosaurs!", and swap the wheat joke for a fruit that bees do pollinate, such as apples or strawberries. Also hedge the ancient-honey line and attribute the one-in-three bites to pollinators.
Vary the speech tags beyond giggled and laughed, and soften the opening "She did not care" into something cosier that still sets up the adventure.

scenarios.why: F13: 15-minute band C on space-race. The longest target - tests that length does not become padding.
scenarios.best_moment: "That's not a rocket," Theo said. "That's a skyscraper that's mad about something."
scenarios.worst_moment: Theo let out a long breath he hadn't realized he was holding, then grinned.
editor_notes: Turn Theo from commentator into participant. Give him a hands-on job in more chapters, such as tuning the radio to catch Sputnik's beep, holding Leonov's tether line, or reading the Apollo 13 fix steps aloud. Use the unused word budget (target up to 4,800) to build the 'mysterious' thread around the cube and who Byte really is.

Tell the Laika story honestly for a 10-year-old. Drop 'Don't worry' and say gently that she did not come home, which is why she is remembered. Also fix the sound inconsistencies, such as the bark that 'echoed' after the story teaches that space is silent.

Cut the repeated clichés ('breath he hadn't noticed he was holding' twice, 'filed/tucked it away' twice, 'steady/careful as anything'). Replace the bolded Band-A shout-along lines with a sharper, older-kid running joke.

scenarios.why: F13: a sensitive-but-allowed topic, band B. Must pass with scary_level <= 1.
scenarios.best_moment: "He's like a lighthouse," Maya said softly. "Steady, even when it's stormy."
scenarios.worst_moment: He stayed until every last passenger was safely aboard a boat, brave the whole night through.
editor_notes: Fix the factual softening. Replace Captain Smith 'stayed until every last passenger was safely aboard' and 'nobody's hurt' with a gentle, honest line suitable for band B (for example, 'not everyone could get into the boats, and that's why the rules changed'). Move Molly Brown's boarding to Cherbourg or simply meet her later on deck.

Pay off the 'nearly unsinkable' setup by letting Maya see the ship go down calmly from the lifeboat and recall the word 'nearly'. This gives the story its emotional spine and makes the 1985 discovery land harder.

Give Maya an active beat in Chapter 7, such as helping Molly Brown row, drawing the Carpathia's light, or swimming-themed talk that uses her third stated like. Attribute the shout-lines so a parent knows who is shouting.

scenarios.why: #48: A5 cell. A three-year-old, the youngest band edge, on a gentle science topic.
scenarios.best_moment: Ivy cupped her hands and opened them wide, like letting a little bird go free. "Bye bye, light!" she called, waving.
scenarios.worst_moment: "Like clapping my yellow paint and my blue paint!" she said.
editor_notes: Add the missing colour-splitting beat between Chapters 4 and 5. As the light pops out, it fans into red, orange, yellow, green, blue and purple, and Ivy paints each colour as Splash names it. This is the heart of the topic, it plays directly to her love of painting, and it would bring the length up into the target range.

Merge or untangle Chapters 6 and 7 so the sun appears once and the rainbow arrives at a single clear moment. Give Ivy an action that plausibly 'makes' it happen, or change Splash's line to 'You found a rainbow, Ivy.'

Replace the yellow-and-blue paint analogy, since mixing those makes green, not a rainbow, and could confuse a painter. Cut the told-feeling lines ('She was not scared one bit', 'She felt proud') in favour of actions.

scenarios.why: #48: A5 cell. A note about a bedtime fear - the story must soothe it, never feed it.
scenarios.best_moment: "The dark is not scary," Hoot said gently. "It is just nighttime, wearing its soft black coat."
scenarios.worst_moment: Leo smiled. Taking care of sleepy things felt good.
editor_notes: Thread Leo's fear of the dark through the middle chapters: let him notice the night getting friendlier at each stop (for example, owls and bats loving the dark), so the ending relief is earned rather than stated.
Cut or simplify the abstractions for a five-year-old. Drop the year 1953 and the jargon 'REM', and replace 'ninety minutes' with something concrete like 'about as long as a movie'.

Remove or fix the unsupported owlet-versus-baby comparison, add the growth fact to the True Facts list, and vary the stop pattern so one station gives Leo a real choice or surprise rather than another imitation.

scenarios.why: #48: A10 cell, the widest mixed ages (3 and 11). Band A words, but the 11-year-old still needs a reason to listen.
scenarios.best_moment: "Nobody beats gecko toes," he said. "Not one lizard. Not one bug. Not even a very determined three-year-old."
scenarios.worst_moment: "No," said Willow gently. "That bug is just resting. The spider will let it go soon."
editor_notes: Fix the two factual slips. Remove the claim that the spider will let the trapped bug go: put the bug beside the web rather than in it, or have Willow say gently that this web is empty today. Rewrite Isla's climbing line: climbing shoes use smooth, sticky rubber, and chalk keeps hands dry, indoors and out.

Give the animal parade a shape instead of looping on 'Next climber?'. Fold Chapter 2 into Chapter 1, use the girls' tiny size so they try each trick themselves, and build to a final climb where Isla and Rosa combine what they learned. That would also lift the word count into the 1,300–1,700 range.

Cut most of the giggling/laughing dialogue tags and drop the repeated 'Rosa had no idea what that meant' beat. Give Rosa a shout-line or idea of her own in those spots so the three-year-old gets her own wins rather than just reacting to her sister.

scenarios.why: #48: A15 cell (was empty), and a third story in the Milo and Juno series. The longest band A target - padding is the risk.
scenarios.best_moment: "Why not? You keep a hundred LEGO bricks in your bedroom."
scenarios.worst_moment: "T. rex liked a good snack too," Bricky said, smiling.
editor_notes: Fix the T. rex scene. Keep the tension relief without the false fact by having it snap up a bug, sniff the kids and lose interest, or give a big sneeze, and cut the open-mouth-at-Juno moment so band A has no peril.
Have Bricky model safe behaviour ("Only because this is a magic trip, and only gently, with me here") before the children touch animals. Stop Juno running straight up to a huge wild creature.

Break the identical encounter template in chapters 2-5 by giving at least two chapters a different beat (a choice, a hunt, a small problem the kids solve). Also trim the repeated "grinning" and "best day ever" lines.

scenarios.why: #48: A15 cell. A child who loves spiders and geckos: rule 10 - wild animals are watched, never touched.
scenarios.best_moment: "Mucus," Sam said slowly. "Like frog boogers?" Gordo laughed so hard he nearly fell off the leaf.
scenarios.worst_moment: "This is a friend of mine," said Gordo. "His name is Kellar. He was the first person to explain why gecko feet stick so well."
editor_notes: Fix Chapter 8. Drop the named 'Kellar' cameo, or make the attribution accurate (the 2014 glass climb came from a Stanford team), and give Sam a reason to arrive at the lab. The current scene both misattributes the work and teleports the story.

Hedge or cut the overstatements. Have Gordo correct the LEGO comparison ('Not clicking, more like a magic tiny pull'), soften 'never run dry' and 'never slips', and explain or replace 'hexagons' with 'shaped like tiny honeycomb'.

Break the identical chapter rhythm in the middle. Give Sam one hands-on choice or small problem, such as which way to climb past the ant line or how to cross the wet leaf like the frog, so Chapters 3–7 don't all run animal → fact → shout → goodbye.

scenarios.why: #48: A15 cell. Two small children and bees: rule 10 - nobody pokes a hive or pats a bee.
scenarios.best_moment: "A honey relay race," agreed Clover, smiling. "And nobody ever drops the ball."
scenarios.worst_moment: The honey inside the cell bubbled with tiny golden bubbles as it thickened, almost like it was breathing.
editor_notes: Fix the factual slips. Wax flakes come from under the abdomen, not the wing. Cut the 'bubbling, breathing' honey. Let fanning, not enzymes, do the thickening. Either make Clover a forager or have her scout and then forage.
Remove the stray commas before 'and' throughout ('warm, and sticky'). Thin out the dozen-plus 'giggled'/'laughed Clover' tags so the rhythm reads cleanly aloud.
Turn Chapter 7 into an active beat, for example the kids helping deliver a drop toward the queen. Move the waggle dance before the sealing so the homecoming chapter stays focused on the ending.

scenarios.why: #48: B5 cell (was empty). A BMX fan: rule 10 - no stunt a child could copy without a helmet.
scenarios.best_moment: Omar climbed on and pedaled over the bumps. BZZZT-BZZZT-BZZZT, his teeth rattled. "THAT'S why!" he yelled, laughing hard.
scenarios.worst_moment: "Bikes like this became the standard everywhere," Ding added.
editor_notes: Give Omar a real beat in the Golden Age and Wright chapters. For example, he could race a bloomer-clad rider, or help the Wrights true a wheel and connect it to his own bike. This would keep him driving the scene instead of watching.

Fix the Wright brothers passage. Their bike-shop skills (chains, balance, building light, strong machines) fed into the Flyer, but the plane was wood and fabric, not metal tubes. Drop Wilbur's knowing 'In 1903.'

Push the requested 'funny' tone with more jokes that land for parent and child, and with BMX wordplay tied to each old bike. Replace the shout lines that merely echo dialogue with fresh call-and-response moments.

scenarios.why: #48: B5 cell, a new topic. Small magnets are a real swallowing hazard: the story must not make them a toy to put in a mouth.
scenarios.best_moment: "That way's north," Snap said. "Also, that way's the bathroom."
scenarios.worst_moment: "Wood's tiny bits point every which way," said Snap. "Messy crowd. No wave. No magnet."
editor_notes: Fix the science in Chapters 3-4 and in True Fact f5. Explain that iron's tiny groups point every which way until a magnet comes near and lines them up, while wood and plastic don't have those magnetic groups at all. Drop 'the tiniest building block there is' for atoms, since the next breath puts electrons inside them.

Don't model a 6-year-old snapping a magnet apart. Broken magnets make small, swallowable pieces, which are a real hazard for children. Let Snap split himself, or a grown-up's demo magnet, to show both halves keep two poles. Keep the battery-and-nail coil clearly as Snap's trick rather than something Ada copies.

Turn Chapter 8's whispered fact list into one more Ada moment, for example her toy robot floating on a pretend maglev track. Then place 'Stick together!' only where it fits, such as magnets clicking or Ada and Snap teaming up, so the catchphrase and the silly tone both land.

scenarios.why: #48: B5 cell. Siblings who tease: rule 9 - affectionate teasing, never an insult a child could repeat.
scenarios.best_moment: "You can't just declare a winner!" "I'm six. I can do anything."
scenarios.worst_moment: "Enter, bend, bounce, bend, exit," said Splash. "Four steps. One rainbow."
editor_notes: Fix the viewpoint logic in Chapters 6-7: the children cannot look up at a rainbow from inside a raindrop. Pop them out onto a cloud or back above the lawn before they see the full circle and the second bow.

Turn Splash's lectures into kid-driven discovery. For example, Dev turns his back to the sun and squirts to make his own rainbow, proving the "sun behind you" rule with his favourite toy. Priya could spot the flipped colours of the second bow herself instead of being told.

Tighten the details: fix "Four steps" (it lists five), replace the repeated "water squirter" with a livelier word, strip the [fN] tags from the facts list, and swap "Splash made it better" for a callback such as Priya starting her hula-hoop painting.

scenarios.why: #48: B10 cell. The two failures the judge caught on sharks and volcanoes at once: teasing siblings (rule 9) and wild animals (rule 10).

notes: judge reported a guardrail breach

scenarios.best_moment: Jack squeezed his own ear. "So sharks are basically made of ears?"
scenarios.worst_moment: "Souvenir," she announced, "from the biggest fish ever to scare absolutely nobody, because it isn't even here anymore."
editor_notes: Remove the touching of wild sharks, which breaches guardrail rule 10. Finn instructs Jack to 'Touch — gently — from front to back' on a great white, Jack 'tapped the shark's snout' on the hammerhead, and Ellie strokes the whale shark. Have the children feel denticles on a shed tooth or on Finn himself, or observe from a safe distance, and let Finn say real divers never touch.

Use the parent note that Jack and Ellie wind each other up. Give them an affectionate, mutual running tease, for example Jack insisting 'mermaid's purse' is a silly name until Finn sides with Ellie, so the sibling dynamic shapes a scene.

Tighten chapters 5-7 and fix the ending's continuity. Give each species stop a hands-on beat or choice rather than a sighting-plus-fact. Decide who holds the fossil tooth and correct 'a hundred million years ago, give or take.'

scenarios.why: #48: B10 cell, a new care topic. A town lost to a volcano, told to a 7-year-old: true, and calm.
scenarios.best_moment: One tile felt warm. It was blue-green, smaller than a stamp. It began to hum, low and soft, like a kettle thinking about boiling.
scenarios.worst_moment: "Maybe you just did," said Tessa, winking, "by noticing it."
editor_notes: Fix the continuity seams in Chapters 6-7. Either keep the bread in the oven as Nora finds it, or move her into a museum on purpose, and make the jump from grassy hillside to active dig a deliberate time-skip. Also make the fountain one thing, either a face or a fish.

Give Nora one moment where her mosaic know-how changes what happens. For example, in Chapter 3 or 6 she could spot or complete a pattern Tessa missed, or choose where to go next. That would turn her from a curious listener into a driver of the plot.

Tighten the facts and the rhythm. Hedge the date ("Romans wrote August 24th, though clues suggest it may have been autumn"), change "thousands of years" to "almost two thousand years," and either give every chapter its shout-along line or drop them, so the pattern doesn't fizzle out after Chapter 2.

scenarios.why: #48: B15 cell (was empty). Maya's series continues with Barnacle, and Apollo 1 is a care fact at age 7.

notes: narrative word count 1558 is outside 2400-3300 ±15%

scenarios.best_moment: "That's everyone you know," said Barnacle, "on one little ball, floating in the dark."
scenarios.worst_moment: Maya let out a breath she didn't know she was holding.
editor_notes: Bring the length up to at least 2,400 words by giving Maya hands-on beats rather than more facts. For example, she could help talk Apollo 13 home by sketching a workaround, or try to steer the bath-boat alongside Vostok 6. This fixes the length and breaks the drift-by-and-ask pattern.

Open with a callback to the last story (Barnacle's flipper wave and the bridge's final rivet), and give Barnacle at least one bad pun per scene ('a re-markable launch', 'out of this whirled'), as the bible specifies.

Correct Apollo 13: the crew didn't fix the tank, they cleverly used their little lunar lander as a lifeboat. Also cut stock phrases like 'a breath she didn't know she was holding' and vary the repeated waving.

scenarios.why: #48: B15 cell. Where the volcanoes scenario broke rule 10 (a stick in a hot spring) - now for a child who collects rocks.
scenarios.best_moment: "I made the Ring of Fire. Out of my rock collection." "You did," said Cinder, grinning. "Not bad for a Tuesday."
scenarios.worst_moment: In 1815, it had the biggest eruption ever recorded, bigger than any other volcano, before or since.
editor_notes:
Fix the factual errors:
- Tambora was the largest eruption in recorded history, not ever.
- Mauna Loa's height should read about 4,170 m above sea level, or about 9 km from the seafloor.
- Seismographs were already in use before 1980; say monitoring improved.
- Olympus Mons is about two and a half Everests tall.

Lighten the disaster load and give Chapter 8 a single hands-on beat in place of four quick stops:
- Merge or soften one of the three casualty chapters.
- Use Zara's unused love of crystals, for example by having the geode reveal crystals that formed from volcanic fluids, or by having her find obsidian.
- Let her discover something herself, not just ask questions.

Clean up the read-aloud problems:
- Reassign the shield-volcano explanation in Chapter 3 to Cinder, or have Cinder clearly prompt Zara for it.
- Drop the invented brother, which may not match the real child.
- Vary the repeated 'held Cinder close' beats.
- Attach the bold shout lines to a speaker so the child knows when to join in.

scenarios.why: #48: B15 cell. A long story on a topic the children know better than the writer - accuracy and no brand worship.
scenarios.best_moment: "Technically," said Byte, "you're player one of all time."
scenarios.worst_moment: "Sony's new PlayStation uses these instead of cartridges," Byte explained.
editor_notes: Repair Level 9: give the PlayStation its own beat with a year (1994-95), have Ben hold up the disc it refers to, and add a matching True Facts entry for it and for the Wii.

Fix the factual slips. Drop 'first... against a friend' from Spacewar! or reframe it as one of the first games on a general-purpose computer. Hedge or remove the 'two straight days' claim. Move Pajitnov out of the 1985 US toy store, for example to a quick stop in Moscow. Either mention E.T. in the landfill scene or remove it from the True Facts list.
Trim the repeated doorway-humming tags and stock lines. Spend those words on one more Ben-specific joke or Minecraft/pixel-art callback, and fix the Byte size inconsistency.

scenarios.why: #48: C5 cell (was empty). The shortest band C target - a lot of history in few words.

notes: gate reported 1 hard violation(s)

scenarios.best_moment: Lena, who had spent her whole career catching things with her hands, raised an eyebrow. "Except the goalkeeper. Please tell me there's an exception for the goalkeeper."
scenarios.worst_moment: "From a muddy field in England to a room full of countries arguing in French. That's a wild ninety years."
editor_notes: Give Lena something to DO in the league/FIFA and World Cup chapters. For example, she could help McGregor sort the fixture list, or face one Pelé shot in goal, so these scenes stop being fact relays she merely comments on.

Fix the chronology and continuity slips. Put the 1930 World Cup before the Lily Parr/1991 sequence, change 'Back in London,' and replace 'a wild ninety years' with a figure that matches the dates shown.

Make the Pickles reveal land. Have the guide state outright that the real 1966 hero was a dog named Pickles, and treat it as true rather than 'local legend.' Also trim the doubled bold shout-line and phrases like 'untouched by physics.'

scenarios.why: #48: C5 cell. A child who fights bedtime: persuasive without lecturing, and ends sleepy.
scenarios.best_moment: "It's also why doctors say nobody should ever try to beat it," Luna said firmly. ... "Interesting story. Terrible plan."
scenarios.worst_moment: "It's a owl giving a very obvious hint, yes."
editor_notes: Give Arjun something to do in the middle stops, not just questions to ask. For example, he could adjust the master-clock gears with a flashlight beam, bowl a ball that gets 'filed' onto the memory shelf, or choose which animal to visit. This would break the exhibit-tour rhythm of Chapters 4-6.

Turn the reported-speech fact dumps into dialogue or action. Chapter 1's 'She told him that in 1953...' and Chapter 5's trophy-case recital could be scenes in which Arjun watches the eye-twitch experiment or reads the Nobel plaque himself.

Clean up the details: fix "It's a owl" to "an owl", add Randy Gardner (and the third-of-life fact) to the True Facts list, remove the [f#] tags, and soften 'skipping sleep is basically skipping growing' to something more accurate.

scenarios.why: #48: C5 cell. An older child on an invention story - mystery tone without inventing facts.
scenarios.best_moment: "That's not a bike," Tom said. "That's a unicycle that swallowed a trampoline."
scenarios.worst_moment: "Nicely saved," the rider said, impressed. "That might be a slight exaggeration of how graceful you looked. But you stayed up."
editor_notes: Rebuild Chapter 8 around one or two moments Tom experiences, such as feeling a derailleur shift on a hill or glimpsing the Marin County riders, instead of a remembered list of statistics. Then make sure every fact that stays also appears in the True Facts list.
Lean into the requested mysterious tone. Give the spoke a puzzle or rule (why it chose Tom, what it 'remembers') that pays off when it goes dim on the workbench.

Give Tom something to do in Chapter 6 beyond asking questions, for example helping the cyclist free a skirt caught in her chain so that bloomers make sense. Also fix the garbled 'slight exaggeration' line in Chapter 3.

scenarios.why: #48: C10 cell. The Titanic for a 10-year-old: more of the truth than band B, still bedtime-safe.
scenarios.best_moment: A fake funnel for show. She liked that this enormous, serious ship had one small bit of showing off built right in.
scenarios.worst_moment: Phillips tapped a pattern: dash-dot-dash-dash, dot-dot-dot-dash. "CQD," he said.
editor_notes: Fix the factual slips. Correct the CQD Morse to dash-dot-dash-dot, dash-dash-dot-dash, dash-dot-dot. Move the funnel-counting scene to Southampton, where the ship has funnels and the smoke makes sense. Cut Molly Brown's invented 'cabin' line, and either add the 'Unsinkable' nickname to the story or drop it from True Facts.

Give Hana at least one choice that matters inside the history. For example, she could guide a frightened child to a specific boat in Chapter 6 on the page instead of in summary, so she acts rather than only witnesses.
Delete the orphaned bold echo lines at the ends of Chapters 2 and 4, and keep just one closing line. Add a touch of band-C dry humour, such as a wry crew remark, to balance the solemnity.

scenarios.why: #48: C10 cell. Competitive brothers: rule 9 - rivalry without put-downs.
scenarios.best_moment: Max pressed two bricks together. They wobbled, then slid apart. "Almost," he said, "is doing a lot of work in that sentence."
scenarios.worst_moment: A boy about Max's age wandered past, testing a set with careful, serious hands, like he was grading it.
editor_notes: Fix the Kjeld scene. He was about 30 in 1978, so either show him as an adult taking the reins in 1979, or move the 'boy testing toys' beat to the 1950s, when he really did test toys as a child.

Rebuild Chapters 6 and 8 around a hands-on beat or choice for the boys, such as a LEGOLAND ride, a DUPLO click test, or being asked what the struggling company should cut. Then the years arrive through action rather than announcements from unnamed staff.

Vary or cut the repeated brick-pulse chapter endings. Also cut the clichéd 'breath he hadn't noticed holding' and the leftover '**IT HOLDS!**' line, and replace the 'half the planet' hyperbole with something true.

scenarios.why: #48: C15 cell, a care topic at length. Honest about what happened, never graphic.

notes: narrative word count 2728 is outside 3300-4800 ±15%

scenarios.best_moment: Pompeii didn't get to finish its sentence. Which is why, almost two thousand years later, people like you get to come back and read the rest.
scenarios.worst_moment: with a different kind of material — hot volcanic mud instead of ash. It kept things ash never could: wooden furniture, even scrolls of paper, still readable.
editor_notes: Add roughly 300–700 words to clear the length floor. Spend them on a mystery Isla actively cracks with the glass, for example decoding the baker's stamp on the bread or a cheeky wall graffito. This would deliver the requested 'mysterious' tone and turn her from a questioner into a solver.

Fix the factual slips. Herculaneum was buried by pyroclastic surges and flows, not mud. Its scrolls are carbonized and only now being read with scans. Plaster casting began in 1863, so signal a time jump before chapter 6. Hedge the August 24 date ('the date in Pliny's letters; some newer clues suggest October').

Let the eruption chapter carry some excitement within band C limits, for instance a moment where Isla must choose to hold the glass steady as the ash thickens, instead of 'We're safe… Just watching.' Also trim the repeated 'real archaeologist' phrasing and merge the two 'Tomorrow' endings into one last line that lands.

scenarios.why: #48: C15 cell. Theo's series continues on a new topic: Bit and the coins must come back.
scenarios.best_moment: "I made a friend," Theo said, breathing hard. "Different scoreboard."
scenarios.worst_moment: Theo watched a sparrow dart past a second later, chasing the same bug the raptor had been eyeing.
editor_notes: Fix the geography and timeline errors. Move Argentinosaurus to Patagonia and Spinosaurus to North Africa (or make Level 7 a world map tour). Separate Stegosaurus from Triceratops; Bit could even joke that more time separates them than separates T. rex from us. Give Stegosaurus four spikes. Cut the sparrow from the Cretaceous scene.

Fix the Mary Anning scene. Have her describe 'sea dragons' or 'great lizards' rather than 'dinosaurs', name ichthyosaurs instead of mosasaurs, and replace the invented dog legend with her real dog Tray. Also have Theo stay above the waterline, for example passing her a tool or spotting the fossil, rather than wading into crashing surf at a cliff base.

Break the end-of-level formula and trim the verbal tics. Vary how the coins appear, resolve the Sue hologram-vs-solid-tooth contradiction, and cut most of the 'basically's and the stray bold banner lines.

scenarios.why: #48: band D (13-17), which F13 never covered. A teenager must not be talked down to.
scenarios.best_moment: "That's not possible," Eli said out loud, to no one, which is a thing people say right before something answers them.
scenarios.worst_moment: HE SOLVED IT HIMSELF, TEN MILES UP!
editor_notes: Fix the factual slips. Explorer 1 launched about eight months before NASA began operating, not four. Leonov was hundreds of kilometres up, not 'ten miles'. Saturn V stages were thrown away, not 'brought back down controlled'. The Apollo-Soyuz docking happened closer to 140 miles up than 200.

Let Eli's radio and physics skill drive at least one or two scenes instead of Relay narrating everything. For example, he could work out why Leonov's suit ballooned before Relay explains it, or reason through the Apollo 13 power problem, so the story depends on what he does rather than what he hears.
Cut the all-caps shout lines, which are out of register for a 14-year-old. Vary the repetitive 'Relay said, [date]' openings and repair the garbled closing sentence about the radio looking useless.

scenarios.why: #48: band D. A 15-year-old who likes the numbers side of the game.
scenarios.best_moment: "Best piece of scouting in football history," the Gaffer agreed.
scenarios.worst_moment: Tomorrow's practice couldn't start soon enough — she had a whole new column to add to the spreadsheet.
editor_notes: Put the ball at Mia's feet: let her try a cuju flick, get swept into the mob football and take a touch, or use her stats instinct to make a choice that changes a scene. That way she plays the history rather than watching it from the sideline.

Fix the two factual slips. Change "except for a gap during the world wars" to the single Second World War gap (1942 and 1946), and change "two hundred years too late" to roughly 140. Also avoid showing both cards to one player in 1970; no red card was actually shown at that tournament.

Tighten the shape. Cut the band-A shout-lines, pay off "forty more stops" and the Gaffer's "One more" with a real final stat or twist, and replace the redundant last line with something that lands, such as a callback to "Forty-four years between titles. One good dog. One traffic light."

scenarios.why: #48: band D, short. A teenager who stays up on a phone: why sleep matters, without a sermon.
scenarios.best_moment: Noah, who had assumed sleep was basically a loading screen, leaned in and asked the obvious gamer question: "So what's actually running while the screen's off?"
scenarios.worst_moment:
"Respect,

**Respect to the sleep genes.**
editor_notes: Repair Level 5. Finish Noah's broken "Respect," line and give the chapter a real beat, such as Noah spotting the clock gene in action or asking the scientists a question, instead of a three-line stop.

Give Noah things to do, not just things to say. Let him tweak a monitor, sort a memory on the librarian's shelf, or choose which room to enter, so each level is something he plays rather than a lecture he comments on.
Make the True Facts list match the story. Remove f3 (REM muscle paralysis) or add it to the plot, add the bat and fruit-fly facts, hedge the glymphatic claim, and fix the garbled fruit-fly sentence.
